Power tariff rationalization 
*410. SHRI CM. IBRAHIM: Will the Minister of POWER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) what steps have been taken for rationalization of power tariff in Andhra 
Pradesh, Maharashtra and Kamataka in the context of agitations against high power 
tariffs in Andhra and other States, through Central Electricity Regulatory Commission 
or State Electricity Regulatory Commission or otherwise; and 
(b) whether State Electricity Regulatory Commissions have been set up in 
these States, if so, the composition and functions thereof and if not, in which States 
steps are being taken to set up State Commissions? 
THE MINISTER OF POWER (SHRI SURESH PRABHU): (a) and (b) The 
Electricity Regulatory Commission (ERC) Act, 1998 has paved way for 
establishment of Regulatory Commission at the Centre and the State with a view 
to rationalisation of electricity tariff, transparent policies .regarding subsidies, 
etc. Under the provisions of this Act, the Central Government has constituted the 
Central Electricity Regulatory Commission (CERC). Maharashtra has 
constituted State Electricity Regulatory Commission (SERC) under the ERC Act, 
1998 while Andhra Pradesh and Kamataka have constituted SERCs under their 
respective State Reform Acts. The SERCs in all these three States consist of three 
Members including Chairperson. Sixteen other States have also constituted SERCs. 
So far 11 State Commissions have issued tariff orders. 
CERC has been entrusted with the powers inter alia to determine tariff for 
Central Generating Companies and inter-State Transmission Companies etc., while 
SERCs have been given power inter alia to determine tariff for electricity, wholesale, 
bulk, grid or retails as the case may be within the State. 
Under the ERC Act, 1998 the State Electricity Regulatory Commissions, 
while fixing tariff are to be guided by the principle that tariff progressively reflects 
the cost of supply of electricity at an adequate and improving level of efficiency 
and if the State Governments so desires it can grant subsidy to any consumer or 
class of consumers in the tariff determined by SERC by paying the amount to 
compensate the utility affected by grant of such subsidy. 
Andhra Pradesh Electricity Regulatory Commission (APERC) announced its 
first tariff order which was made effective in June, 2000. There had been an 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
average tariff increase of 15%. The tariff order sought to reduce cross subsidy and 
link tariffs to cost of service. For domestic consumers average tariff was increased 
by 54%. However, to mitigate the impact of tariff increase on residential 
consumers, the Government provided additional subsidy of Rs. 281 crore. Total 
subsidy paid by .the Government of Andhra Pradesh during 2000-01 is Rs. 1626 
crore. The APERC has issued second tariff order on 24.3.2001 proposing no tariff 
hike for the year 2001-02 except minor adjustment of tariff for domestic consumers. 
Government of Andhra Pradesh has committed subsidy of Rs. 1561.41 crores 
during 2001 -02. 
Maharashtra Electricity Regulatory Commission (MERC) in its first Tariff Order 
dated 5th May, 2000, has directed that the tariff for ail categories would be 
simplified and would be gradually moved towards cost of supply. In tariff proposal 
for 2001-02 in the pursuance of MERC's order, MSEB has tried to rationalize the 
tariff by reducing 40 Nos. of categories/tariff rates to 17 Nos. Also subsidy 
deviation from cost of supply which was between 30% to 141% has been brought 
down to 38% to 125%. 
Kamataka Electricity Regulatory Commission (KERC) has issued its first 
tariff order which has made effective from 29th December, 2000. The average tariff 
increase was equivalent to about 17% as against the hike of 24.5% proposed by 
Karnataka Power Transmission Corporation Ltd. (KPTCL). Government of 
Kamataka have agreed to give an additional subsidy of Rs. 144 crore to give relief to 
agricultural consumers below 10 Horse Power (HP). 
Acquisition of auto pilot system 
*411. SHRIK. RAMA MOHAN A RAO: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of DEFENCE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is fact that the CAG has criticised the Ministry and the IAF for 
not speeding-up the acquisition of auto pilot system for jaguars and 
upgradation programme of MIG-21 aircraft; and 
(b) if so, the reaction of Government thereto? 
THE MINISTER OF DEFENCE (SHRI GEORGE FERNANDES): (a) and (b) 
Report No. 8 of 2001 of the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (CAG) has 
pointed out delays in upgradation programme of Jaguar and MiG-21 BIS aircraft. 
10 

[ 19 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
The need was felt in 1985 for an autopilot for incorporation into the Jaguar 
control system. Autopilot equipment during the eighties was of large dimension 
and it could not be integrated in the Jaguars. In the nineties, smaller systems 
were available and a decision was taken to install the autopilot. A contract was 
concluded in August' 1999 for supply of autopilot systems with associated 
spares. Work for integration of this equipment is in hand. 
A contract was signed with Russia in March 1996 for upgradation of MiG-
21 BIS aircraft. The programme is expected to be completed by 2004-2005. The 
delay has been due to key avionics syst ems not having been develped as per 
expected time frame and because of problems of import procedures in Russia. 
Two aircraft upgraded in Russia have now been positioned at Hindustan 
Aeronautics Limited (HAL), Nasik and are undergoing test flights.

*413. SHRI NILOTPALBASU: Will the Minister of HOME AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have taken note of the controversy arising out of the 
first application of the POTO in Jammu and Kashmir; 
(b) if so, the details of the case and the views of the State Government 
thereon; and 
© whether Government are forwarding some advice to the State 
Government on this development? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRICHENNAMANENIVIDYASAGAR RAO): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(c) The State Government of Jammu and Kashmir has informed that, on 
22.11.2001, a raid was conducted on the residential house of one Gh. Mohammad Dar 
s/o Mohammad Abdullah Dar R/o Safakadal, Srinagar on the basis on an intelligence 
input that terrorists had established a hide-out in the said house. During the 
operation, a substantial quantity of arms/ammunition, explosives, etc. were recovered 
and five persons including Gh. Mohammad Dar were arrested. 
13 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
Invoking the provisions of the Prevention of Terrorism Ordinance, 2001 (POTO), a case 
FIR No. 218/2001 was registered at Police Station, Safakadal (Srinagar). The house 
in question was sealed as the initial investigation led to the belief that the hide-out had 
been constructed out of the proceeds of terrorism. Upon a further legal examination 
of the issue, it was found that only a part of the house, being used as a hide-out of 
terrorists, could be reasonably believed to have been constructed out of the 
proceeds of terrorism and not the entire house. It was, therefore, decided that the 
seizure of the house was not warranted in this case and the house was accordingly 
restored to the family. 
The State Government has further informed that action has been taken to dispel 
fears and remove apprehensions voiced by a section of the public and political 
parties about the likely misuse of POTO. 
(c) No, Sir.

Reforms in mining sector 
3044. SHRISOLIPETA RAMACHANDRA REDDY: Will the Minister of 
COAL AND MINES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether there is a proposal under active consideration of the Union 
Government to introduce reforms in mining sector/coal mining sector to effect 
a major change during the Tenth Plan period; 
(b) if so, the details thereof in all respects; 
(c) when the reforms are expected to be initiated; and 
(d) how far it shall improve the mining conditions/coal production and 
reduction in prices thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COAL AND MINES 
(SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD): (a) to (c) The major reforms initiatives are 
as follows: 
1. The Coal Mines (Nationalisation) Amendment Bill, 2000 has been 
introduced in the Rajya Sabha with the following objectives: 
(i)   To allow the Indian Companies to mine coal and lignite in the country 
23 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
without the existing restriction of captive mining. In other words, the 
objective is to allow the Indian companies in public and private sector 
to mine coal and lignite and also to sell the same in the open market. 
(ii)   To allow the Indian Companies in the public and private sector to be 
engaged in exploration of coal and lignite resources in the country. 
The purpose is to augment production of coal in the country through 
association of the private sector with the existing nationalised coal sector to 
bridge the demand and supply gap assessed for the Xth and Xlth plan period. 
2. Recently the Government have revised the coal mining policy of 1979 
spelling out the conditions under which the State Government undertakings 
can do coal mining. Under the revised policy, the State Government companies 
or undertakings are allowed to do mining of coking and non-cocking coal or 
lignite reserves, either by opencast or underground method, anywhere in the 
country. 
3. The Mines and Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act, 1957 which 
govern the mining sector including coal and lignite, was last amended in 
December 1999 and subsequently two principal Rules, viz, Mineral Concession 
Rules, 1960 and Mineral Conservation & Development Rule, 1988 have been 
amended thrice in a bid to simplify the procedure for grant of mineral concession, 
to attract more and more foreign direct  investment in mining sector and to 
delegate more and more powers to the State Governments, who are the owners 
of the minerals. Therefore, reforms in mining and coal sector is an ongoing 
process. Total number of Foreign Investment Promotion Board's (FIPB) approval 
in the mining sector is 70; the foreign equity component of the approval is 
approximately Rs. 4,000 crores. 
4. Two Working Groups-one on Mineral Exploration and the other on 
Coal and Lignite-were constituted by the Planning Commission to make 
recommendations for the Tenth Five Year Plan. The two Working Groups have 
submitted their reports to the Planning Commission. 
(d) Reforms should attract higher investment, better technology and more 
skilled manpower should foster competition and better management practices; 
should keep the domestic mining sector to face international competition; and 
above all; should promote delivery of better products and services at more 
competitive prices to the consumers.

3100. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have decided to set up a National Disaster 
Management Agency (NDMA); 
(b) if so, the details alongwith its terms of reference; and 
(c) the immediate steps taken/proposed to be taken by Government to 
prepare a data base on infrastructure and facilities relating to disaster 
management? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
I.D. S WAMI): (a) to (c) In the context of the developing security situation, the need

backed up by a professional pool of manpower, has been felt by the Government. As 
proposals regarding the requisite structures and capabilities are presently in the 
formative stages only, it is too early to furnish any further details in this regard.

Girls' Trafficking in Delhi 
3102. SHRI S. RAMACHANDRAN PILLA1: Will the Minister of HOME 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the news-item titled "Attapadi's 
unwed mothers tell a tale of tribal exploitation" appeared in the Hindustan Times, 
dated the 28th November, 2001; 
(b) if so, the reaction of Central Government thereto; 
(c) whether of late the cases of minor girls ending in trafficking nets are 
reported in the Press often daily and the Capital has become a great victim for it; 
and 
(d) if so, the steps taken by Government to curb this bad practice 
throughout the country? 
THE MINISTER OFSTATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI 
I.D. SWAM1) (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. However, the Government of Kerala has stated 
that no incident of turning murders into suicides or rape being treated as willing 
sex in the police records has come to its notice. 
(c) It is incorrect to state that the Capital is turning into a center of trafficking 
in minor girls. The Delhi Police has been taking strict legal action as and when 
any such incident is reported. As a re sult of the concerted efforts to combat 
trafficking, the Delhi Police rescued 191 minor girls during the year 2001 (upto 
30.112001). 
(d) 'Police' and 'Public Order' are State subjects as per the Seventh Schedule 
to the Constitution of India and as such, registration, investigation, detection 
and prevention of crime including that against women and children is primarily 
the responsibility of the State Governments. 
The Central/State Governments have been implementing a number of 
projects/schemes for the rescue and rehabilitation of women and children affected 
by the flesh trade either through their own agencies or in collaboration with 
NGOs. These schemes include a scheme called 'Jabali' in Madhya Pradesh which 
aims at assisting the voluntary organizations to take up activities for the welfare 
65 

RAJYASABHA [19 December, 2001] 
and development of women and child victims; the Devdasi Rehabilitation Scheme of the 
Kamataka Government; a project started by Government of Andhra Pradesh for 
rehabilitation of women victims who are infected with HIV, the Maharashtra Government 
have set up Special Juvenile homes which are counselling facilities vocational training 
and health care for children affected by commercial sexual exploitation and 
HIV/AIDS. 
Besides, schemes for training, employment and income generation like 
Integrated Rural Development Programme (1RDP), Jawahar Rozgar Yojana(JRY), Support to 
Training and Employment Programme (STEP), Setting-up T/aining-cum-production 
Centres (NORAD), Socio-Economic Programme (SEP), TRYSEM and DWACRA 
are implemented in source areas for the welfare and rehabilitation of prostitutes. In some 
of the red light areas the Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) Schemes have 
been launched. The Government has an extensive network of Short Stay Homes and 
homes set up under the Juvenile Justice Act for protection and rehabilitation of the 
victims of prostitution.

maintain status quo in the area pending

1951 and their percentage of total population; 
(b) the State-wise and year-wise other communities and their population 
included in the Scheduled Lists of the Constitution from 1951 to 2001; 
(c) whether it is a fact that population of SC and ST at present is higher 
than reservations provided for various purposes; 
(d) if so, whether Government propose to provide higher representation in 
Parliament, State Assemblies, Panchayats  and services in proportion to their 
population; and 
(e) if so, by when it will be provided and if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
(SHRI CHENNAMANENI VIDYASAGAR RAO): (a) and (b) The details of 
State- wise and census year-wise (1951 -1991) population of Scheduled Castes, 
Scheduled Tribes.and Other communitie>fNon SC/ST) and ujeir percentage to 
total population are given in Statement I to V (See below). The population of 
Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes as per the 2001 Census are not yet 
available. 
(c) to (e) As per 1991 Census of India the percentage of Scheduled Castes 
and Scheduled Tribes in the country, excluding Jammu and Kashmir, was 16.48 
and 8.08 respectively. Percentage of reservation for SCs and STs in services 
68 

[ 19 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
under the Central Government in case of direct recruitment on all India basis 
by open competition is 15 per cent and 7.5 per cent respectively. In case of direct 
recruitment on all India basis otherwise than by open competition reservation 
for SCs and STs is respectively 16.66 per cent and 7.5 per cent. In case of direct 
recruitment to Group C and D posts which normally attract candidates from a 
locality or a region, percentage of reservation for SCs and STs is generally fixed 
in proportion to the population, of SCs and STs in.the respective States/UTs. 
In case of promotion, 15 per cent posts are reserved for SCs and 7.5 per cent 
for STs, provided the element of direct  recruitment, if any, does not exceed 
75 per cent. 
It is stated that reservation for Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and 
OBCs in services under the Government of India is already 49.5 per cent and 
50 per cent in case of direct recruitment on all India basis by open competition 
and on all India basis otherwise than by open competition respectively. Under 
the circumstances revising the percentage of reservation for Scheduled Castes 
and Scheduled Tribes as per their population, is neither contemplated under 
Article 16(4) of the Constitution nor feasible, as such revision would make the 
total reservation for SCs/STs and OBCs in excess of 50 per cent. 
Constitution (Ninety-first Amendment) Bill, 2000 was introduced in the 
Lok Sabha on 27.11.2000, seeking to extend the existing constitutional embargo 
on undertaking fresh delimitation of electoral constituencies upto the year 2026 
AD and simultaneously to undertake readjustment and rationalization of 
constituencies in the States, without altering the number of seats allotted to 
each State in the House of the People and Legislative Assemblies of the States, 
including the Scheduled Caste and the Scheduled Tribe constituencies, on the 
basis of the population ascertained at the census for the year 1991 as also to re fix 
the number of seats reserved for the Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes 
in the House of the People and Legislative Assemblies of the States on the basis 
of the population ascertained at the census for the year 1991, was passed by the 
Lok Sabha on 21.8.2001 and by the Rajya Sabha on 23.82001. The said Bill is now 
in the process of being ratified by the State Legislatures before receiving the 
assent of the President under the provisions of the Article 368 of the Constitution. 
Pursuant to its enactment the Government will further bring a legislation which 
will provide for setting up of an authority to carry out the purposes of the 
aforesaid Constitution Amendment Bill. 
As regards reservation of seats in the PanchayatsTthe same is governed 
by Article 243 D (1) of the Constitution of India.

'Police' and 'Public Order' are State subjects as per Seventh Schedule to 
the Constitution of India. As such, registration, investigation, detection and 
prevention of crime is primarily the responsibility of the State Governments. 
However, the Central Government has been adivising the State Governments, 
from time to time, to give more focussed attention to the improvement of 
administration of Criminal Justice System. Information relating to the busting of 
immigration rackets by the local police is not maintained centrally. 
Improvements in the security features of Indian Passports and Visa stickers 
to minimize tampering are undertaken on a continuing basis. All immigration 
staff also exercise vigilance in this regard and are given special training and 
equipment to scrutinize travel documents to ascertain their genuineness. New 
security features in the passport are introduced from time to time to make them 
tamper proof. 
(c) and (d) No formal study has been carried out by the Central 
Government. However, it has come to the notice of the Government that the 
modus operandi adopted by illegal immigrants traveling on forged passports 
includes departure from Kathmandu or smaller airports in India being used for 
international travel. Many countries including Cyprus, Malta and Thailand 
provide visa on arrival. Many illegal migrants prefer to proceed to these countries 
first and then target some other countries. A number of them also use complicated 
routes through several countries using a combination of land and air passage 
and purchasing documents along the way.

should meet the cost of using this technology.

New Policy regarding captive power plants 
3134. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA : Will the Minister of POWER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether a new policy regarding captive power plants has been drafted 
to facilitate full utilization of installed capacity of these plants; and 
(b) if so, the progress on the finalization of this policy? 
† Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
105 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2001] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF POWER (SHRIMATI 
JAYA WANTIMEHTA) :(a) and (b) The State Governments have been requested 
to encourage setting up of captive generations mechanism plants and to create 
an institutional mechanism which may allow captive power units an easy entry 
into the power sector by quickly clearing captive power applications, giving the 
developers a rational tariff for purchase of surplus power by the grid and third 
party access for direct sale of power to other industrial units. Under Secton 44 
of the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948, the State Electricity Boards (SEBs) given 
consent to setting up of captive power plants by various industries irrespective 
of the capacity of such plants. Consultation of Central Electricity Authority is 
necessary only in cases where the captive power project exceeds 25 MW. 
On July 11, 2001 the Minister of Power has circulated a Captive Power 
Policy prepared by the Ministry of Power in consultation with the CEA to all the 
State Governments and Union Territories. In this policy, the following has been 
included: 
• If captive plant is of Hydro or cogeneration, such plant, irrespective of 
its size, may be permitted liberally. 
• If captive power plant is based on coal or liquid fuel or gas such plant 
may be allowed and capacity of the plant permitted upto 200% of the 
requirement of industry (If the state is deficit in power). 
• Captive power plant may be allowed if State/SEB or successor entity 
are unable to supply the required power supply. Such a captive power 
plant can be considered for the uninterrupted power supply to the 
industry even if the State is surplus in power. 
• If the industry required quality power supply which is not available, 
the proposal for installation of  the captive power plant can be 
considered. 
• If the cost of generation from captive power plant is found to be lower, 
the proposal may be considered after examining the cost and tariff. 
• Units in Special Economic Zone (SEZs) and industrial entities may be 
allowed to set up captive power plants liberally. 
• Bank facilities are propose to be provided to CPPs. The rates for banking 
may be determined on mutualy agreed terms. 
106 

[ 19 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
•   Prior approval of SEB has to be obtained for wheeling of power. 
Wheeling may be done to any service (HT or LT). Wheeling charges 
may be worked out based on pooled rates worked out by Central/State 
Transmission Utility of that region. 
• The tariff for sale of power from thermal and hydro CPPs, may be fixed 
after mutual discussion and could be based on pooled variable charge 
of thermal power stations operating under the SEB plus some percentage 
of the pooled variables charges as incentive. Tariff could also be based 
on the highest variable cost in the system or actual variable cost of 
CPP, whichever is lower and some percentage of the variable cost as an 
incentive. 
• Third party sale is also permissible with the approval of SEB.

concerning the health and scientific management of the country's land resources. 
It does not have any fixed term and has only ex-qfficio Members, as indicated 
above. The Council has held only one meeting on 6.2.1986 and the decisions 
taken, relating to Wastelands Development, at this meeting, are given in the 
statement. 
Statement 
Decisions taken at the first meeting of the National Land Use and 
Wastelands Development Council held on 6.2.1986 relating to 
Wastelands Development 
1.     Identification of Wastelands 
1.1  The State Governments should id entify wastelands in forest areas, 
revenue common land or degraded farm land. 
12    At least 5% and 20% of these wastelands should be utilised in 1986-
87 and in the Seventh Five Year Plan respectively for afforestation, 
development of pasture and forest-based industries. 
2    Nodal Agency 
A nodal agency/mechanism should be  created in the State for (a) 
coordinating, funding and activities re lating to different schemes of 
afforestation and wastelands development; and (b) for monitoring and 
evaluation of the various schemes. 
3. State Seeds Corporation 
The work of the State Seeds Corporation should be extended to include 
the production and supply of fodder, grasses and legume seeds on a 
commercial basis to farmers. 
4. Direct Seeding 
4.1 Seeds, suitably pelletised, to enable the retention of mulches and 
hydrogels, should be distributed to growers with suitable instructions 
for sowing. 
124 

[ 19 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
4.2    In remote and difficult areas, in critical watersheds and ravines, aerial 
seeding must be considered. 
5. Leasing of Land 
The State Government must lay down clear guidelines for the leasing 
of forest and non-forest wastelands to the rural poor. 
6. Urban Fuel wood and Green Belts  
The State must set up a machinery for providing a green belt of fuelwood 
and fodder plantations around towns and cities. 
7. Degraded Forest Areas 
7.1 The State Forest Department must identify degraded scrub forest land 
which must be broadcast with fodder and legume seeds, so that the 
resultant fodder may be used by the local people, keeping in view that 
an estimated one million hectares of scrub forests in the country is to 
be brought back to green cover each year. 
7.2 Degraded forest area must be used to raise fuelwood plantations to 
provide for the use of the local community, through their involvement. 
8. Forest Development Corporations 
The State Forest Development Corporation must not confine itself to 
exploitation of forest produce. Fuelwood and fodder plantations, both 
within the degraded forest area and in wastelands outside, must be 
actively undertaken by the Forest Development Corporation with the 
help of institutional finance. 
9. Forest-Based Industries 
9.1 Forest-based industries should not only be encouraged to afforest 
wastelands with a view to secure  raw material but also make a 
commitment to undertake fuelwood and fodder plantations for the use 
of local communities on a part of the land leased to them. 
9.2 Industries must also enter into agreements with small farmers for the 
supply of their raw material needs on a viable basis. 
9.3 Such plantations must be raised on wastelands distant from habitations, 
so as not to disturb existing community use. 
125 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
10. Government Department/Public Sector Undertakings of the States 
and Central Governments 
10.1 Government departments/undertakings in possession of substantial 
areas of unutilised land in their control, should cover these areas with 
tree/fodder cover. 
10.2 Railway sides, road sides and canal sides must also be afforested at the 
cost of the Departments concerne d, who should provide a specific 
allocation therefor. 
11. People's Involvement 
11.1 Nurseries: The social forestry programmes should lay greater emphasis 
on people's involvement through nursery relating and farm forestry. 
By 1987-88, at least 50% of the total seedings in each State should be 
raised through people's nurseries, i.e., kisans, schools, women and 
youth groups. Further, such nurseries should also be specially 
decentralised so that a nursery is available within a 10 km. radius. 
11.2 Sapling Distribution: A uniform policy of distribution of sapling at a 
minimum price of 10 to 20 paise should be considered, the prices 
being gradually increased to its real value. It must be recognised that 
free distribution is counterproductiv e to emergence of free market 
operations in sale of saplings. 
11.3 Farm Forestry: Farmers should be encouraged to plant saplings on 
their field-bunds or farms. 
 
11.4 Tree Grower's Cooperatives: Tree Grower's Cooperatives must be 
promoted which should provide inputs and technical guidance and 
also make arrangements for harvesting and marketing. 
11.5 Tree Pattas: The State must formulate a Tree Patta Scheme, wherever 
such a scheme is not already in fo rce. A specific target for the year 
must be prescribed and achieved. 
11.6 Strip Plantations: The State Government must consider introducing a 
tree patta scheme for lessing given strips of land for plantation on 
roadside and canalside. 
11.7 The State Government must simp lify the procedure for the Tree Patta 
Scheme. 

[ 19 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
12. Media and Communications 
A massive campaign must be launched to involve the people in 
afforestation and wastelands development. Pamphlets and posters may 
be issued and distributed through Panchayats and Block Development 
Officers on how to raise nurseries, select species, get land lease, get 
bank finance etc. The need is to use all available and possible media 
to make it a people's movement. 
13. Akashvani and Doordarshan 
Akashvani and Doordarshan must develop suitable programmes to 
be broadcast on a regular basis and involve public figures in 
spreading the message.  
14.    School Curriculum 
The curriculum of the schools should include a better understanding 
of land resources, causes of its de gradation wastelands development 
and afforestation. 
15. Monitoring and Evaluation 
Effective steps need to be taken to strengthen the database on which 
policy formulation and monitoring and evaluation of programmes 
can be undertaken. 
16. Remote Sensing Applications Centre 
Remote Sensing Applications Centres must be established in the State, 
wherever not in existence already,  to provide data on resources — 
land, water, mineral, trees, etc. Su ch data may be computerised for 
easy storage and retrieval. 
17. Funds 
All possible ways and means must be exploited — including avenues 
of institutional finance — for the afforestation programme.  
18. Laws 
All Acts relating to planting and harvesting of trees, leasing of land, 
Usufruct Rights, etc. should be examined in the context of amendments 
that may be called for to motivate the rural poor and other institutions 
for afforestation. 
127 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
19.     Role of Government Departments. 
19.1   Policies need to be formulated and enforced so that those who are held 
responsible for degradation and wh o contribute to the increase of 
wastelands are held accountable for re-foresting the degraded lands. 
19.2  Irrigation projects, mining, hydro-electric projects etc. must be 
considered only if sufficient safeguards are built in so that no new 
wastelands are created. Wherever th is is not feasible, compensatory 
afforestation of wastelands must be undertaken by such Projects.

Statement-III 
Recommendations of the study report on consolidation of land 
holdings 
• The scheme of consolidation of land holdings should be formulated 
with reference to uniformity of soil conditions, farm infrastructure, spatial 
features, cropping partem and perceptions on the market value of the 
land specific to each State in a participatory manner. 
• The Policy should address the in stitutional issues like credit, 
technology, marketing, extension and managerial support to the farmers 
accepting the scheme of consolidation of land holdings. 
• The consolidation of land holdings is to be considered as a State subject 
and there is need to organize the State resources to implement the 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [ 19 December, 2001 ] 
scheme. The central schemes with financial support need not be called 
for to implement the scheme on consolidation of land holdings in various 
States. 
• The States need to formulate regi on specific approaches for the 
consolidation process and should use bottom-up strategies taking the 
concurrence of the farmers. 
• The Panchayats or the local bodies in the State may be empowered to 
implement such schemes. 
• Cooperative farming practices for pooling the land of small and 
marginal farmers need to be en couraged for the commercial and 
horticultural crops as an alternative to the consolidation of land 
holdings. 
• The cooperative farming also manifests largely the objectives of the 
consolidation of land holdings and need to be encouraged wherever 
possible as an alternative to the consolidation of land holding scheme. 
• The success stories of the cooperative farming may be studied and the 
farmers may be motivated for such  experiments for better yield and 
income through the land. 
• There is a strong feeling amongst the farmers that the consolidation 
officers do not take the concurrence of the farmers before confirming 
the scheme and such actions resulted in resistance among the farmers 
to accept the scheme. The concurrence of the farmers on the scheme 
before confirmation needs to be sought in the Gram Sabha. 
• The capacity building exercise need s to be taken up by the Central 
Government for the State Departments chosen to implement the 
sponsored schemes. 
• Confidence needs to be built among the farmers who were already 
covered in the consolidation scheme in some States and are now 
facing post-scheme implementation problems. 
• The scheme of consolidation of land holdings need to be popularized 
among the farmers. 
• The centrally sponsored scheme(s) on consolidation of land holdings 
may be continued in the State on case by case basis assessing their 
132 

[19 December, 2001] RAJYASABHA 
interest in implementing the scheme. Capabilities and competencies in 
delivering the services to the farmers. 
• There is a need to give thorough rethinking on the scheme of 
consolidation of land holdings, as there were many administrative 
and socio-economic hurdles experienced in the past. The scheme may 
be considered on case-by-case basi s in consolidating the wasteland 
for improved agricultural practices. 
• It is necessary to develop some animators from the farmers community 
to generate awareness about the scheme in their peer group. This would 
also help in building strong inter-personal communication base for 
implementation of the Government schemes in the villages. 
• The Gram Sabhas may be used as the platform for disseminating the 
communication on the schemes and their benefits on consolidation of 
land holdings and computerization of land records. 
• The communication campaign may be planned through the interface 
with officials at Gram Sabhas, displaying posters, highlighting success 
stories on consolidation of land holdings and the like. 
Computerization of Land Records 
• The Centrally Sponsored Scheme on the Computerization of Land 
Records has been well received by all the States as they had initiated 
the process of CLR despite some administrative problems. This Scheme 
should continue and all the States need to be covered under this Scheme. 
However, the States may be advise d to meet the recurring costs on 
management of the database. 
• States showing low response like Bihar and Uttar Pradesh may be 
motivated to speed up the work on CLR. There is need for periodical 
intervention of the Government of India to monitor the progress of 
the CLR work, assess the extent of utilization of grants and delivery 
mechanisms to the farmers. 
• The updating of land records by each VAO on schedule needs to be 
encouraged and strict measures have to be imposed thereof. 
• In the process of computerization of land records periodical updating of 
data is a major task and need to perform with all sincerity. This has 
been the major problem at the village and block/tehsil/mandal levels in 
133 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December, 2001 ] 
the States due to administrative reasons. The VAOs are often over-
burdened with variety of responsibilities and could not attend 
satisfactorily to the land records assignments on time. It is suggested 
that the Governments of all States may launch a campaign on updating 
the land records data at the district level during lean agricultural season. 
At least four months in an agriculture year, preferably the lean season 
may be declared as the land records updating period. This could help in 
concentrating on this specific task and complete within scheduled 
period. 
• There is an immediate need for improving computer skilled staff in 
the talukas where there are no operators to manage the systems. There 
are large numbers of vacancies sanctioned by the State Governments 
but they are not yet filled in many States. This is leading to severe 
human resource bottleneck in carrying out the scheme. 
• The compulsory training to the staff at the taluka and district levels 
need to planned for carrying out th e computerization task of land 
records and also the office automation with the existing system 
support. 
• Security measures for the land records data need to be ensured, as it is a 
very sensitive document. The security of the data at the level of 
updating or modification needs to be ensured, as this is absent in all 
the States except in Gujarat. The NI C has to be apprised of this need 
and necessary provisions have to be developed in the package. 
• The data back-ups need to be taken after every update and need to be 
stored in Compact Disks. The use of catridge tape drives (CTD) may 
be gradually replaced by CDs. The co pies of the taluka-wise data in 
CDs need to be kept also at the district level with the office of the 
Superintendent of Land Records or an equivalent competent authority. 
• The maintenance of the systems at the remote places is enormously 
delayed due to accessibility proble m. The companies assigned with 
the annual maintenance contract of the system in a district should be 
asked to appoint resident engineers and sufficient staff for providing 
timely service support. 
• There is need to set-up dial up links with the talukas to the district 
headquarters through networking of the system. The accessibility of 
134 

[ 19 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
the land records data may also be made available to the office of the 
Commissioner Land Records of the State. 
• The linkage needs to be established for on-line data transfer from the Office of 
the Land Registration Authorities in the State/district/taluka to the land reforms 
department, which has taken up the task of computerization of land 
records. Such on-line transfers of land registration would help in up-
dating the land records data faster. 
• The States need to be encouraged to start the process of the delivering 
computerized Record of Rights to the landowners and confidence among the 
farmers about its authenticity and validity need to be developed involving 
concerned officials and local leaders. 
• Presently every State follows its own way of computerization of land records. 
The data variables are different for each State and so the out also is largely 
customized. This is despite the fact that most of them adapt NIC software. 
Consequently, their contents, quality of information and process of 
computerization is amenable to the interstate comparison. Hence there is a 
need for standardizing the format of computerized record of rights across 
the States for developing standardized package of land records. It is 
strongly recommended that a common software need to be developed and 
common variables may also be identified for the record of rights and village 
profile to enable the standardized computing process throughout the country. This 
would help in knowing the right measure and extent of land records in all 
States and maintaining the database. 
The digitization of cadastral maps needs to be done in a more scientific manner 
using appropriate packages. The maps need to be generated in the system by giving 
the scales and not be dependent on the scanning all through the process of digitization. 
There is also a need for updating the survey maps before initiating the digitization 
process in all the States.

Identification of habitations affected by water quality problems 
3158. SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: Will the Minister of RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any survey has been made to identify the habitations affected 
by water quality problems; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the strategies evolved to ensure that these habitations have access to 
genuine potable water? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF RURAL 
DEVELOPMENT (SHRI SUBHASH MAHARIA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. Water quality 
survey was made initially during 1991—94. The same was reviewed and revised 
by the States during 1998-99. Accordingly, as on 1.4.1999 the total number of 
water quality affected habitations stood at 217211. Details of water quality 
affected habitations State-wise and quality-wise is given in the Statement (see 
below). 
140 

[ 19 December, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(c) Rural drinking water supply is a State subject. State Government take 
up schemes/ projects for providing drinking water in rural areas. Government of 
India supplements the efforts of the State Governments and provide financial 
assistance under Accelerated Rural Water Supply Programme (ARWSP) and 
Pradhan Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY) —Rural Drinking Water (RDW). 
Under ARWSP, up to 20% of the allotted funds can be utilised to tackle water 
quality problems. 
The strategy evolved to ensure provision of safe water supply in rural 
habitations include: 
I.    Replacement of contaminated spot source by a new one at appropriate 
location; 
II. Mini Piped Water Supply Scheme based on problem free deep tube 
well; 
III. Surface water based piped water supply scheme; and 
IV. Treatment of quality problems through suitable removal unit. Besides 
advocacy of dual water supply system in endemic quality habitations

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF TEXTILES (SHRI V. 
DHANANJAYA KUMAR): (a) to (c) The Textile Package as announced by the 
Government in the Union Budget for 2000-01 is for the whole country and is not 
State-wise. The provisions regarding duties and taxes contained in the package 
are in implementation with effect from the date on which the Budget came into 
force. The Package is meant to stimulat e the growth of and investment in the 
textile industry. The Package include s duty concession and reliefs, higher 
allocation to important schemes and the announcement of new programmes. 
The main points include—  
• Reduction in the basic customs duty on specified textile machines

the weaving, processing and garment sectors.

of Integrated Apparel Parks to enable dereserved readymade garment 
industry to come up with modem units with the best infrastructure; 
• Emphasising funding from the Technology Upgradation Fund Scheme 
for at least 50,000 shuttleless new looms and modernization of 2.5 lakh 
plain looms to automatic looms by 2004; 
• Enhancement of allocation under Technology Upgradation Fund 
Scheme to Rs. 2200 crore from Rs. 50 crore prevailing then; 
• Substantial increase in the Budget allocation for the Ministry of 
Textiles from Rs. 457 crore in 2000-01 to Rs. 650 crore in 2001-02.

have been having this discussion on the statement made by the hon. Home 
Minister now for about seven hours, an d before the lunch recess, we had the 
hon. Prime Minister intervening in the de bate. Now the difficulty of speaking at 
this last stage is that one tends to get repetitive, and also the constraint is that 
the Members, particularly, from the Treasury Benches, are giving us 
unsolicited advice that we must not be acrimonious. I agree with them that the 
situation is such that one cannot be acrimonious on the issues concerned. But, 
I think, it is a very sad state of affa irs that after the statement of the hon. 
Minister and after the interventions of some of the leading Members of the 
Treasury Benches on some of the issues, we are left with a greater sense of 
confusion than clarity. T herefore, what, I think, ought to be discussed by the 
Parliament today is I am not going to  repeat what my le ader and colleague, 
Shri Ramachandran PiHai, has already stated the question of unity. I go back 
to the Resolution which both these Houses adopted on Friday.There were 
three components in it. We condemned the attack; we put on record our 
condolence; we put on record our appreciation for those peopie who have laid 
down their lives and we also

parliamentary system, at any given point of time, unity is bome out of actions

Madam, first of all, I consider it a great privilege to participate in this 
discussion. It comes at a sorrowful moment of the history of this country, when 
the sovereignty of this country itself has been attacked. Terrorism is a virus for 
which there is no medicine. Unless we get rid of terrorism, terrorism will get rid 
of us. It is with that understanding that  we all have to stand to fight this 
malaise. 
Madam, we have been debating this issue for the last two days. 
Some Members said that there was a security lapse and some others said that 
there was no security lapse. I don't want to go into that controversy. But one 
thing comes across my mind and the question that I have asked myself so 
often, ever since that incident happened on 13 th December, is: Could we have 
saved them? Could we have saved those lives? Let us not forget the fact that 
when the terrorists came our Watch an d Ward Staff was without arms. They 
were only armed with their courage; they were only armed with their 
patriotism; they were only armed with  their line of duty; and they became 
victims of that dastardly attack. The onl y thing that I keep on asking myself is: 
Could we have avoided it? The issue is not whether there was security lapse 
inside the Parliament or not. The same  question arises and it has arisen 
several times in my mind even in respect of Kargil. When I think of the fact that 
more than 500 people of our country sacrif iced their lives in the interest of the 
nation, again, the question keeps on ha unting me: Could their lives have been 
saved? The answer is "Yes, those lives could have been saved". Those lives 
could have been saved, if we had kept a vigil. Those lives could have been 
saved, if, as a polity, we were most  sensitiye to the concept of national 
security. If I were to say the words that I am going to say now, people might 
think that I am being partisan. I will quote the words of a person who wrote the 
Kargil Report, Shri K. Subrahmania m, when he talked about the national 
security. This is what he said and I quote: 
"There is a reluctance both on the part of the politicians and the 
bureaucrats to devote time and effort for this purpose. It is 
considered adequate, if people are briefed when the need arises. 
Starting preparations to counter a thre at after it is materialised is the 
surest way of inviting disaster." 
We are starting to counter a threat after it has already materialised. 
We salute those who laid down their lives with courage. But we must 
introspect. Not the Government alone, we as a nation must introspect. Have 
we in the last decade or so taken note of the concerns of national

friends and hon. friends who have spoken, that this is not the time or occasion 
for finding fault. I do believe that we are not a fractured Republic. I would like 
to believe that in the face of adversity  and threats, we are a united Republic. 
Our soldiers - Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs -fight bravely; have fought bravely, 
as no one can or has for the entire count ry. This whole country is so full of 
Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs, Christians and a host of other religious communities. 
We are, what we believe, we are. And,  here, I applaud what my distinguished 
and hon. friend, Shri Saifullah, said a few moments ago. What he said was 
well spoken both as a true Muslim and as a true Indian. I submit that we, on all 
sides of the House, must rise above our selves; and our party affiliations. We 
owe this to ourselves, we owe this to th e future destiny of this great country. 
This debate, Madam, is not a post-mortem on the Government or its policies. If 
it was, I would have contributed my ow n views on what I believe to be the 
numerous wrongs of this Government. I have in the past, frequently drawn 
attention to that. But, this is not a post-mortem on the Government. It is a post-
mortem on the dastardly attack on the Parl iament House, as mentioned in the 
statement of the ho n. Home Minister. There is much to criticize about 
Americans and their system of Government. But, at this time, let us, I suggest, 
take a leaf out of the reaction of the si ngle largest party in the United States, 
the Democrats, as large as the Repub licans who are in governance there, at 
the dastardly event s of September 11 th when terrorists took charge on one 
single fnorning of four di fferent American planes at four different places 
leading to catastrophic events, thousa nds of deaths in New York, Washington 
and elsewhere. These terrorist acts were all as a result of what we would have 
called very loudly, obvious security lapses.  But the lips 
236 

[19 December 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
of each and every democrat were sealed. Why? Not because they excused 
the Bush Government for vital security lapses, but only because they wanted 
to present a united front in fighting terrorism. 
If I mentioned America, it was only because it is the oldest 
democracy in the world and ours is the largest democracy in the world. What 
has happened has happened. What has been spoken and done, whether by 
the Prime Minister or leaders on all sides,  whether in Bombay or in Delhi, has 
been said and done. Today, when we are debating the stat ement of the hon. 
Home Minister, we represent, I believe, the entire country. We do not - I would 
suggest - represent any particular politic al party. Post-December 13 in India, 
like post-September n m in the United States, is a different period of political 
history or as the Americans may like to can it, post-December 13 is a different 
ball-game. Please, consider this fact, I beseech you, that the Leader of the 
House was yesterday able to read the hon. Home Minister's statement, on the 
events of December 13 th, and we have been privileged to discuss it both, 
yesterday and today is simply "miraculou s". Those of us who believe in God, 
as I do, must thank him for this deliverance. But, no deliverance comes 
without a price. And we have paid the price by losing heroic lives. I believe, 
we must all show that we, as a body, are worthy of that deliverance. 
As the poet says: "The Moving Finger writes; and, having writ, Moves 
on; not all thy Piety nor Wit. Shall lure it back to cancel half a Line, Nor all thy 
Tears wash out a Word of it." So, let us look ahead. The Home Minister has 
rightly said in the very first paragraph of the Statement read out yesterday that 
the country would always remain indebted to the Security personnel who 
made the supreme sacrifice. He is right in  saying so. We will, but let us reflect 
how we will remain indebted to the memo ry of those brave saviours. I suggest 
that it is only by continuing our deb ates and discourse; by continuing the 
business of this House without disruption and with tolerance for one another's 
views, howsoever, divergent they may be. Thus, we must show to the world 
that we, in our heart of hearts, genuine ly believe in Parliamentary system of 
democracy. If we come to this House and do not spend time in the business of 
the nation - debating great and cont entious issues - even the ordinary 
intelligent people will come to the conclusion that there is a little need for a 
Parliament. Let us never, by our actions or omissions, give our people this 
impression of Parliamentary democracy . The Statement of the hon. Home 
Minister has asked us to ponder why terrorists and their backers tried to raise 
the stake so high, and 
237 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December.2001] 
has suggested an answer in paragraph 9. I would venture, Madam, to add a 
rider to this. The reason why the terrorists and their backers tried to raise the 
stakes so high by attacking this instit ution was that because those behind the 
terrorists are envious of our Parliamentar y system of Government. It is, as the 
hon. Leader of the Opposit ion rightly said, the heart of our democracy. It is 
also the envy of our neighbour. It is simply  because this country alone, in this 
entire sub-continent has continuously enjoyed a Parliamentary system for over 
50 years. Those who masterminded the terrorist attack of December 13, 
wanted to get at our heart, because they could not dare to see or to tolerate 
the survival of this great nation. I sa y all this, Madam, not on my own, but on 
the authority of a fine Parliamentari an whom I had the good fortune to know, 
and greatly admire, the late Piloo Mody. Shri Piloo Mody had visited Zulifikar 
Ali Bhutto, who was his friend, in a prison in Pakistan awaiting a sentence of 
death for murder a murder of which it was widely believed, and it is still widely 
believed, he was innocent. Shri Piloo himself told me and has also recorded 
this that in his conversation with Bhutto in the Pakistan prison, Bhutto 
nostalgically recalled what he called, and I quote "the noise and chaos of 
Indian democracy", and he deeply regre tted that he had made f un of it in the 
hey-day of his political power. The noi se and chaos of Indian Parliamentary 
democracy, he had told Piloo Mody, has a certain vitality; it has the strength 
and safety of numbers. No citizens' fa te, no legislative measure, depended on 
the whim or dispensation of one man.  Bhutto was right. Look around, hon. 
Members, I beseech you, at our neighbour  and then thank our lucky stars that 
despite all our faults and drawbacks of  our Parliamentary system, rt has 
always ensured in these past 52 years a peaceful change of governments both 
at the Centre and in the States. This is the discipline of the Parliamentary 
system of Government of which we are proud and of which others make fun. It 
is only because they are envious of our Parliamentary democracy. Madam, the 
expressions in the stat ement like "the most aud acious" and "the most 
alarming" do require some response, and the Government has to make up its 
mind about what it will do and keep its powder dry. But, I believe, we demand 
too much by asking the Government to disclose its hand today in so vital a 
matter that affects the security of the nat ion and relations with foreign States. I 
would respectfully say to the leaders in Government, consider all your options, 
in whichever order you consider them most appropriate, but never on the basis 
of party politics.  That is the bottom line. 
238 

[19 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Madam, I would conclude by saying, as the Prime Minister has 
rightly told us late this morning that the need of the hour is wisdom. The 
statement of the Home Minister recalls the address to the nation of the Prime 
Minister on the 13 th of December, and he declared that the fight against 
terrorism has reached a "decisive" phase. I only hope and pray that whatever 
decision that is taken to fight this ghastly new facet of terrorism, the 
Government will be guided, not by impu lse, not in anger, but with wisdom.  
Thank you, Madam. 
SHRI CHO S. RAMASWAMY (Nominated): Madam, I shall try to 
finish my speech within the four minutes  that are allotted to  me. I think, the 
time allotted to me is only four minutes. Madam, but for the courage and the 
presence of mind shown by the security men and Watch and Ward staff, we 
would have had an immense problem on our hand, the kind of problem which 
we had not seen or experienced befor e. And, Madam, who would have been 
blamed for that; not the se curity staff, but the Go vernment. Everyone would 
have ruled the Government unfit to govern. Now, when such a disaster has 
been averted, why should we grudge in  giving a share of the credit to the 
Government? I think this has become a convention with us. When there is a 
plane crash or a train accident, the Government is blamed and the Minister, in 
all probability, will have to go, but when  a plane crash is averted or a train 
accident is miraculously averted, the credit goes to the person concerned, the 
man on the spot, and not to the Government. This is the unfairness of the 
established convention, based on the concept of moral responsibility. I am not 
trying to divert the attention from the gratitude the nation owes to those brave 
people who have laid down their lives. The least we MPs could do is, to 
contribute, as substantially as we c an, to the fund that is already being 
organised. I, Madam, on my part have already undertaken to contribute one 
year's salary to the fund. 
Now, we are talking about the security arrangements not being 
enough. But what is now demanded, a fter the attack, would not have been 
tolerated before the event. For exampl e, if before the event, every car was 
stopped at the gate and fully checked a nd the MPs were asked to get down 
from their cars and walk to the Parliament, would it have been accepted 
without protest? I think, everyone would have talked about harassment and 
humiliation. Only after the event, we rea lised the seriousness of the situation, 
and then we say that security arrangemen ts were not enough.   Let us also 
not forget that the U.S., with all its modern 
239 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December,2001] 
gadgetry and sophisticated telecom equipment was not able to foresee or 
unearth the plan to attack the Twin Towers. Not only that, our security 
agencies have been able, within a matter of days, to unravel what happened 
really. They have given almost in a chorological order the various stages of the 
conspiracy that led to the attack. We have to praise them for it. We have to 
praise the system also for it, not only the men who are handling* it. And, we 
have to praise the Government also which has made it possible to happen. 
Madam, now, about what comes next -- I am not a military expert like the 
General is, nor am I foreign affairs expert -- I have to rely on common sense. I 
feel that we must give peace a chance,  and that could be done by expecting 
the Alliance against terrorism to discipl ine Pakistan. We have to give them 
some time, but if they are not willing or if they fail to do that, then after genuine 
efforts after sincere efforts, then, we  may have no other option except direct 
action. That may mean crossing the LoC and may mean inviting a war. But if 
only a war can achieve peace for us, then, it be so. We must be prepared for it 
at that stage. But before that, I think, it will be wise to give peace a chance. If it 
is not taken, then, wage a war to ac hieve peace. Madam, apart from other 
things, this attack on the Parliament has brought a semblance of unity to the 
Parliament itself, to the House, and to  the proceedings. During the last week 
the two Houses were immersed in total turmoil. Now, the Government is 
prepared to say that the O pposition has to be consulted. They are prepared to 
concede It, the right of t he Opposition with some re servations. The Opposition 
is prepared to concede the fact that t he Government cannot place all its cards 
on the table; and it has to hold back vital information. Well, at least, this kind of 
an understanding between the Opposition and the Government has become 
possible only after the attack. In that way, the attack has brought peace to the 
Parliament. I am sure, it will bring peace to the country. Thank you. 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: I would rather have turmoil in the House 
than that kind of peace. Shri B.J. Panda. 
SHRI B.J. PANDA (Orissa): Madam  Deputy Chairman, in paying 
homage to the martyrs of 13 th December, 2001, I would like to express my 
gratitude not because they have sacrif iced their lives, but because they 
sacrificed their lives for upholding the dignity and preservation of the 
parliamentary system of democracy wh ich Mr. Nariman has so evocatively 
spoken about. When I learnt about the bravery and the sa crifice of these 
people, particularly Shri Yadav, t he image that haunts me is an unarmed man 
with a family to take care of running after a car and trying to stop it, a car filled 
to the gills with explosives and weapons. 
240 

[19 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
Madam, I would like to compliment the hon. Leader of the Opposition 
for what I can only describe as his statesman like response to the statement of 
the Home Minister. In particular, I would like to commend him for his explicit 
statement to the effect that  this was not the time to apportion the blame, this 
was not the time to point the fingers. The theme of solidarity has been echoed, 
again and again, throughout these two days of debate. I compliment all those 
hon. Members who have furthered this  theme both from the Opposition 
Benches as well as from the Treasury Benches. In this light, I personally 
hesitate to make the fine distinctio n between the personal bravery of the 
security people and the Watch and Ward staff and the security arrangements 
themselves. Madam, they are undoubtedly personal bravery also. They are 
part and parcel of the security drill of looking for suspicious vehicles, for 
looking out suspicious people and taking  action to stop them. This is what 
these brave men did. 
When we talk about security, a great onus lies on us, the Members of 
Parliament. Have we not all seen examples of some Member or the other 
browbeating the same brave people on occasions at being questioned or 
stopped or simply for not being recognised? Have we not seen examples of 
some Member or the other taking an offence to their companion being stopped 
and searched? Madam, the onus is on us, not just words, but the way that we 
can honour these martyrs is to help in  strengthening the system of security. 
We must be prepared to sacrifice some of our facilities within this Parliament 
complex which will bring some degree of inconvenience to us. But that is the 
only way to honour these brave people; and  that is the only way to strengthen 
their very hands. In this connecti on, many suggestions have been made. 
Perhaps, all the cars should be parked at a distance; and the ferry bus system 
be operated to bring Members into the Parliament House. Perhaps, smart 
identification cards could be utilised which every Member ought to agree to 
wear prominently. Perhaps, fingerprint scanning systems can be implemented. 
There should be no distinction between the depth of the security procedures 
that ought to be followed here and that of those followed at any airport, for 
instance. We do not have even the minimum level of security screening. 
Perhaps, we ought to agree to having fewer entries into Parliament. It 
becomes simpler to control and to manage. In any case, when we talk of 
security, we ought not to think only of the Parliament Complex; we ought to 
think, as has been said in the last two days, of the entire country. This requires 
a cultural change; this requires a change  of national attitude, that we must set 
an example first. Some of this is already happening, Madam, at our airports 
since the event of 
241 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December.2001] 
September 11. I have myself noticed many  VI Ps and WIPs themselves being 
open to the idea of being frisked at ai rports. This culture must be spread 
throughout the country for us to continue  to deal with this threat of terrorism 
that is not going to go away, as the hon. Member, Shri Sibal, pointed out. 
The issue of solidarity is very important. Madam, I shall take only a 
minute more. When we talk of solidarity and putting forward a unified face of 
the nation, we must not bicker amongst our selves, we must not find faults or 
point fingers at our own faults, but look at the outrageous claims that are being 
made across the border. Pakistan has made the outrageous claim that this 
attack was engineered by India itself. That is what we ought to be all taking 
on, in every forum available to us. Madam, I endorse the diplomatic efforts that 
have been suggested by so many hon. Members. But, in pursuing diplomatic 
efforts, pursuing the friendship and the cooperation and support of 
neighbouring countries, is equally important  as pursuing all those of the sole 
super-power. When it comes to talking about the US' attitude, obviously, the 
statement of their Secretar y of State, concerning th is attack, was blatantly 
hypocritical. But, why are we so reactive? I think we have reached the level 
where we can be far more proactive. In saying this, I heed the advice given by 
General Roy Chowdhury, which is extrem ely important, that  the preparation 
must be made diligently before we can take any action because, apart from all 
the comparisons of 1971, there is one major difference, in that, any action 
today, has the potential of being escalated all the way to a nuclear conflict. 
Madam, just one last bit. We must exercise our increasing 
international influence to arm-twist Pakistan to take action against these 
terrorist outfits. I read in a national magazine last night that the only action that 
has been taken in the last two or three months is that the sign-boards 
proclaiming the terrorist headquarters of the Lashkar-e-Taiba have now been 
taken away, so that, perhaps, it will create a little bit of difficulty for the 
Lashkar-e-Taiba cadres to find their way!  But, that is not the >sort of action 
that we are looking for. If we cannot exercise enough influence to get Pakistan 
to change its ways, then, we must make it change its ways. 
.Madam, in conclusion, I would like to say that I endorse a considered, 
deliberated and prepared-for action. But t hat action must take place and that 
action must be decisive. Thank you. 
242 

[19 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
THE DEPUTY CHAIRMAN: Shri Ma noj Bhattacharya. Manojji, you  
know that you have four minutes. The Home Minister is already there.

the pace of communication can be increase d to a considerable extent. At the 
same time, I also suggest that they should be provided with adequate risk 
coverage. The Government must consider the issue of adequate coverage for 
the Watch and Ward Staff. Since we are talking about terrorismr since we are 
talking about the global phenomenon of terrorism, kindly excuse me for 
making some references, because, I feel  that much of the introspection has 
already taken place in this House, and those issues have already been spelt 
out by many hon. Members,  that instead of reactive , the Government should 
have been proactive. I am sure that the right signal has gone to the 
Government, and they will be plugging the loopholes. I also do not want to 
echo the sense of 
243 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December,2001] 
unity that has emerged over here in this  discussion that the nation is united 
in combating the menace of terrorism, particularly, the cross-border 
terrorism, and the nation is quite united in fighting against any of the 
onslaughts perpetrated unf ortunately by the neighb ouring country of ours. 
But I once again say-l may be repetitive in that sense that on 11 th 
September, the United States of America was caught unaware. They 
perhaps could not comprehend that they would be attacked like this, the

have avoided the loss  of precious  lives of the Watch and Ward Staff, the

personnel.I would say that let us try to address the problem of terrorism at the

you, I would like to urge upon the Go vernment of India that they should 
expeditiously address themselves to these problems. If they are really 
desirous that India should be a count ry where the head is held high and the

India should address the problem of poverty, social alienation and

unless the problem of social evils is taken care of. With these words, I 
conclude.

the vital points of this issue, I make  a request that we should have a small

future generations may remember that there was an attack, and there were 
some brave people who sacrificed thei r lives in protecting the soul of 
democracy, who were willing to sacrifice their lives for protecting democracy. 
Madam, the Home Minister is also here. I make an appeal on behalf of my 
Party, Tamil Maanila Congress, that we should have a kind of monument to

democracy, who were ready to give everything they had, just to keep the

244 

[19 December, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
The other thing is this. Although much has been said and much has 
been told, I would like to remind the House only one sentence which was 
given out by the terrorist group when they missed an attack on the British 
Prime Minister, Mrs. Margaret Thatcher . When the Irish terrorists missed an 
attack, the next day, they  issued a press-release; they sent a message: "Mrs. 
Thatcher, you have to be always lucky, but we have to be lucky only once." 
So, yesterday, or the other day when t he incident took place, we can't ignore 
an element of luck, but for that, t he whole House would have been a 
monument of shambles and fallen pillars to speak to the posterity that the 
greatest symbol of democracy was destroyed by a handful of terrorists. But for 
that element of luck, we should have been very careful. And I would like to tell 
the House that this is not the end; this  is only a beginning. There was a report 
in the newspapers that there was a confusion for one of the accused, that they

would like to tell the Government t hat they had not dropped anything; they 
had only postponed it. 
Yesterday, I happened to listen to  a discussion on the Star T.V. 
During the News Hour, when our Minist er, hon. Jaitley, was discussing some 
issue with Mrs. Ambika Soni, an hon. Member of the House, through the 
media, he was trying to give out as if the Opposition is not cooperative. I am a 
Member of the Opposition, and as a Mem ber of the Opposition, I would like to 
guarantee, and with all confidence and the national fervour in me, I would like 
to say that the Opposition stands with  the Government. Can the Government 
point out a single occasion or a single incident, for the past two-and-a-half 
years, leave alone the domestic issues, when a crucial issue came up and we 
were not with the Government? Immediately after its taking over, when there 
were Pokhran blasts, we had our differences of opinion, like a political party; 
we were never for it, but we just m entioned that the bl asts would create an

quiet. When the hon. Prime Minister made a trip to Lahore, we had our own 
apprehensions, but we never gave out w hat we had in our mind. When the 
Kargil War took place, we were wil ling to point out t hat there was an 
intelligence failure, but 
245 

RAJYA SABHA [19 December,2001] 
you never allowed us to speak for ourselves. You told us, "This is not the time 
to speak. You wait. If you speak, the morale of the soldiers will be spoiled, and 
the country will get a different picture! " We kept quiet. And, then, immediately 
you invited President Musharraf here! We were willing to tell you, "You need

to Kashmir. Now, the enemy is coming an d stareing at the Parliament itself. 
Even then you want us to stand by you. We are prepared to stand by you, if

Deputy Chairman, I have just a few clarific ations to seek. At the very outset, I

here." So, I think there is a bit of cont radiction at the top level. I would be 
grateful if the hon. Home Minister clarifies this point.

voluntarily and immediately gone to t he police with the photographs and the 
documents was held in custody for four days, and that his family was not

report two days back. If this kind of treat ment is meted out nobody is going to 
come forth in the near future and give voluntary information to the police.  I 
would appreciate a comment on this.

by our colleague, Shri Kuldip Nayyar on the I4 m December wherein he 
mentioned that the Watch and Ward staff to ld him during this period that there 
was a proposal to give them arms, but it had been lying with the Home Ministry 
for a long time. Now, is there any such proposal? If there is such a proposal,

VALEDICTORY REMARKS 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members, the Leaders of various political 
parties and groups in the Parliament decided today that after the discussion 
on the attack by the terrorists on the Parliament, the House may now adjourn 
sine die. We are, therefore, adjourning the House accordingly.

RAJYA SABHA [19 December. 2001] 
Before we do so, let us place on record our appreciation for the 
exemplary courage displayed by the security personnel belonging to the 
CRPF, Delhi Police, ITBP and the Watch and Ward, particularly my personal 
security and the two members of the Rajya Sabha Watch & Ward who laid 
down their lives in the highest tradition of devotion to duty and saved the 
Parliament and all of us on the i3m December, 2001. We also wish speedy and 
complete recovery to those who were injured in this ghastly attack. 
Parliament is the temple of democracy and reflects the hopes and 
aspirations of millions of our people. An  attack on this institution is an attack 
not only on democracy which we hold dear but also on the ethos and values 
that we all cherish. The 194 th Session commenced on Monday, the 19 th 
November, 2001, and we have had 21 sittings spread over around 68 hours. 
During the Session, 56 Reports of various Parliamentary Committees 
were presented or laid on* the Table of the House. During the Session, 9 new 
Bills were introduced, 3 Bills were withdrawn, and 11 Bills were passed, out of 
which 3 Bills were repealing Bills and 8 Bills were amending Bills including the 
Constitution (92nd Amendment) Bill, 2001, which ensures seniority in promotion 
of SC/ST Government employees by virtue of reservation. The Government 
Legislative Business took about 12 hours. 
There were 7 Statements by Ministers. Prominent among them were, 
(a) the visit of Prime Minister to Russi a, the United States  of America, the 
United Nations and the United Kingdom ; (b) deliberations and developments 
that took place in the 4 ,h WTO Ministerial Conference held in Doha from 9 ,h to 
13th November, 2001; and, (c) terrorist attack on Parliament House on the 13 th 
December, 2001. 
We had one Calling Attention on the storming of the disputed site at 
Ayodhya by VHP, thereby flouting the Supreme Court directives which lasted 
for three and a half hours. 
We had Short Duration Discussions on the following three subjects 
which lasted for more than 28 hours:- 
(i) Terrorists   attack   on   WTC   in   USA   leading   to   international 
intervention in Afghanistan, its impact on India and its ramifications; 
(ii) Decisions adopted at the 4 ,h Ministerial Meeting in connection with 
WTO negotiations,  recently concluded  at  Doha,  which  have far

 reaching  implications on  agriculture,  textile,  pharmaceutical  and 
chemical sectors etc. of the country; and 
(iii) Growing unemployment in the country. 
We also discussed at length by suspending the Question Hour the 
issues relating to the terrorist attack on Parliament House on the 13 th 
December, 2001, spreading over two days and which lasted for more than 10 
hours. 
Five important matters, with the permission of hon. Chairman and 
three questions of Privileges were raised by some Members which lasted 
about more than two hours. 
There were about 108 Special Mentions on Matters of Public 
Importance. During the Session, 460 Starred Questions, 3180 Unstarred 
Questions were admitted and answered. 45 Starred Questions were orally 
answered and one Statement by Minister correcting the Answer to Question 
was laid. Two Notices for Short Notice Questions and 11 notices for Half-an-
hour discussions were received/admitted, but none could be made. 
During the Session, th ree references were made regarding (a) 
Terrorists attacks in the United States of America; (b) Bomb blast at Jammu 
and Kashmir Assembly and (c) Terrorists attack on the Parliament House. 
We also had All India Conference of Presiding Office rs of Legislative 
Bodies, Chief Ministers of States, Mi nisters of Parliamentary Affairs and 
Leaders of Parties and Whips in the Cent ral Hall of Parliament House on the 
25m November, 2001 to discuss 'Discipline and Decorum in Parliament and 
Legislatures of States and Union Territories in India.' The Conference adopted 
a Resolution encompassing a Code of Conduct for Members of all our 
Legislative Bodies. 
We once again reiterate our resolve to stand united in the face of any 
threat to the unity and integrity of our country and pay our humble homage to 
all those who made the supreme sacrific e in the cause of the nation. I would 
like to take this opportunity to thank the Leader of the House, the Leader of 
the Opposition, Leaders of various parti es/groups and all the hon. Members 
for the kind cooperation extended by them  in conducting the proceedings of 
the House. 
I do so on behalf of the Deputy Chairman, all the Members of the 
Panel of Vice-Chairmen and on my own behalf.
